reading.body:
The legal exposure created by AI training data has been split into ten distinct insurance lines, which means the risk is being priced and traded rather than settled in court.

The ten lines follow the model lifecycle instead of clustering around a single dispute. Three concern data acquisition: defence against class actions over scraping copyrighted training data, liability for harvesting personal data without consent, and collection that is lawful in one country and unlawful where the data originates. Two concern training itself: source code leaking into a public set, and performance collapse from synthetic data carrying hidden errors. Three concern outputs: patent claims against generated content, provenance tools that fail to stop unauthorised synthetic media, and unauthorised voice or likeness. Two sit at the contract layer: whether hyperscaler IP guarantees survive their own conditions, and commercial use that breaches a non-commercial model licence.

For AI, the constraint described here is legal and contractual, not physical. Nothing in the list concerns compute, buildings, or power, so it cannot say whether data rights or electricity will bind first. What it does show is that the right to use training data is being converted into premiums and indemnity terms, which turns an open legal question into a cost a developer can plan around. The line for hyperscaler indemnification in practice is the sharpest item, because it treats vendor IP guarantees as something to be tested against policy conditions rather than assumed.

The list does not say what any of this costs. There are no premiums, limits, deductibles, carriers, or claims, and no indication of which lines are actually written as opposed to merely named. Only one of the ten entries is tied to an outside source. So the data shows how the risk has been carved up for insurance, not how much of it is covered or at what price.
